content: Decisions regarding appropriate nutritional interventions to achieve the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals, particularly Goal 2 (ending hunger, achieving food security, improving nutrition, and promoting sustainable agriculture) and Goal 3 (ensuring healthy lives and promoting well-being for all at all ages), are critical. These efforts also support Member States in meeting global targets outlined in the Comprehensive Implementation Plan on Maternal, Infant, and Young Child Nutrition and the Global Strategy for Women’s, Children’s, and Adolescents’ Health (2016–2030). The recommendations in this guideline are intended for a broad audience, including policymakers, expert advisors, and technical and program staff involved in designing, implementing, and scaling up public health nutrition actions. This guideline aims to facilitate discussions among stakeholders when selecting or prioritizing interventions tailored to specific contexts. It provides key recommendations and summarizes supporting evidence, with further details available in Annex 1 and referenced documents. Nutritional deficiencies, such as anemia and deficiencies in iron, folate, zinc, vitamin A, and iodine, are significant public health concerns, particularly affecting young children and women. The primary causes of micronutrient deficiencies include inadequate intake, poor utilization, or increased losses. Anemia, characterized by a reduced number of red blood cells or low hemoglobin concentration, is commonly caused by nutritional deficiencies, especially iron, but also folate, vitamin B12, and vitamin A deficiencies. Other causes include inherited hemoglobinopathies and infectious diseases like malaria, tuberculosis, HIV, and parasitic infections. Anemia is a severe global public health issue, disproportionately affecting young children and pregnant women. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that 40% of children aged 6–59 months and 37% of pregnant women worldwide are anemic. Low folate levels in women of reproductive age can lead to adverse health outcomes, such as megaloblastic anemia and an increased risk of pregnancies affected by neural tube defects. Surveys conducted between 2000 and 2014 in 39 countries revealed that folate deficiency prevalence exceeded 20% in many low-income countries but was typically below 5% in higher-income countries. Zinc deficiency, often due to inadequate dietary intake or absorption, is also a concern. Severe zinc deficiency, first defined in the early 1900s, is associated with short stature, hypogonadism, impaired immune function, skin disorders, cognitive dysfunction, and anorexia. While severe zinc deficiency is rare, mild-to-moderate zinc deficiency is common globally, with at least 17% of the world’s population at risk, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. Zinc deficiency is linked to approximately 16% of lower respiratory tract infections, 18% of malaria cases, and 10% of diarrheal diseases worldwide. Vitamin A deficiency is the leading cause of preventable blindness in children and increases the risk of disease and death from severe infections. In pregnant women, it causes night blindness and may elevate maternal mortality risk. Vitamin A deficiency is a public health problem in over half of all countries, particularly in Africa and Southeast Asia, affecting young children and pregnant women in low-income countries the most. Emerging health crises, such as the COVID-19 pandemic, exacerbate micronutrient deficiencies, especially among vulnerable populations like children, women, and the elderly. Lockdowns and physical distancing measures have reduced family incomes and access to food, healthcare, and social protection programs, increasing malnutrition and micronutrient deficiencies. Modeling predicts significant impacts of the pandemic on maternal and child undernutrition and mortality, with long-term negative consequences for productivity. Wheat, a staple crop cultivated and consumed worldwide, was first domesticated 9,000 years ago in the Euphrates Valley. Approximately 65% of the global wheat crop is used for human consumption, 17% for animal feed, and 12% for industrial applications, including biofuel production. China, India, and the Russian Federation are the top wheat producers. Low-income countries consume 77% of globally produced wheat and are major wheat importers, with wheat accounting for 24% of imported food commodities in these nations. In 2019, global wheat production reached 765 million tonnes, making it the second most produced cereal after maize and before rice. Wheat flour fortification with vitamins and minerals is a public health strategy to address micronutrient deficiencies. Fortification involves adding nutrients like iron, folic acid, B-complex vitamins, vitamin A, and zinc to improve the nutritional quality of the food supply. This strategy is effective in preventing vitamin and mineral inadequacies and their associated deficiencies. Industrial fortification of wheat flour, when appropriately designed and implemented, is an efficient, simple, and cost-effective method to supply essential nutrients to large population segments. In 2021, 86 countries had legislation mandating wheat flour fortification alone or in combination with other grains. Decisions on which nutrients to add and their quantities should consider the nutritional needs and intake gaps of target populations, usual wheat flour consumption levels, sensory and physical effects of fortificants, type of wheat and extraction rate, availability of other fortified foods, population use of supplements, costs, feasibility, and acceptability by producers and consumers. Fortification programs should include quality assurance and control measures at mills, regulatory monitoring of nutrient content in fortified foods, and assessments of nutritional and health impacts. Centralized milling is desirable for quality control, though not always feasible in some countries. The main objective of this guideline is to provide evidence-informed global recommendations on wheat flour fortification as a public health strategy to improve population micronutrient status, grounded in gender, equity, and human rights approaches to ensure no one is left behind.
